Tyre Wear Patterns: What They Mean

Your tyres tell a story. Learning to read wear patterns helps diagnose problems before they become dangerous.

  1. Centre Wear — Over-inflation or too many motorway miles. Check pressure.
  2. Edge Wear — Under-inflation. Inflate to manufacturer spec.
  3. One-Side Wear — Misalignment or camber roads. Check wheel alignment.
  4. Cupping/Scalloping — Worn suspension or wheel bearings. Check urgently.
  5. Flat Spots — Hard braking or skidding. Replace if cord showing.
  6. Feathering — Misalignment or worn steering head. Check bearings.

UK Legal Minimum: 1mm tread depth across 75% of breadth. Replace at 2mm for safety. Read our Best Motorcycle Roads in Scotland: 15 Must-Ride Routes guide for more. keyTakeaways: Tyre wear patterns reveal underlying problems before they become dangerous.
Centre wear points to over-inflation or too many motorway miles.
Edge wear indicates under-inflation, so inflate to the manufacturer's spec.
Cupping or scalloping signals worn suspension or wheel bearings and needs urgent attention.
The UK legal minimum is 1mm tread across 75% of the breadth; replace at 2mm for safety.

faq.q: What causes a motorcycle tyre to wear in the centre?
faq.a: Centre wear usually means the tyre is over-inflated, so only the middle of the tread contacts the road, or that the bike covers a lot of straight motorway miles. Check your pressures against the manufacturer's specification first. Uneven centre wear reduces grip and cornering feel, so correct the pressure and monitor how the pattern develops.

faq.q: What does edge wear on a tyre indicate?
faq.a: Wear concentrated at the edges of the tread typically points to under-inflation, which flexes the tyre shoulders and generates heat. Inflate to the recommended pressure and check regularly. Persistent edge wear despite correct pressures can also reflect a lot of hard cornering, but chronic under-inflation is the most common and most dangerous cause.

Cupping or scalloping, where the tread wears in a scalloped, wavy pattern, usually signals worn suspension components or wheel bearings. It causes vibration and unpredictable handling, so it should be checked urgently by a mechanic. Ignoring it lets the underlying fault worsen and can make the bike unstable, especially under braking and cornering.

faq.q: What is the legal tyre tread limit in the UK?
faq.a: The UK legal minimum for motorcycle tyres is 1mm of tread depth across three-quarters (75%) of the breadth of the tread. However, wet-weather grip falls off well before that, so most riders replace tyres at around 2mm. Riding on tyres near the legal limit significantly increases stopping distances and the risk of losing grip.

faq.q: Can I fix a tyre wear problem myself?
faq.a: You can correct the most common cause, incorrect pressure, yourself with a gauge and pump, then monitor whether the pattern improves. However, alignment issues, worn suspension, and bearing faults that cause one-sided wear, feathering or cupping need professional inspection. Reading the pattern tells you what to check; some fixes are DIY, others need a workshop.
